entities.summary:
The Greek language, a member of the Indo-European family, emerged in written form during the Mycenaean civilization (c. 1600–1100 BCE) with Linear B script, before evolving into its iconic alphabetic form around 800 BCE. Far from being merely a communication tool, Greek became the primary vehicle for groundbreaking philosophical inquiry, scientific discovery, dramatic artistry, and democratic ideals that profoundly shaped the Classical Era (c. 800 BCE – 600 CE). Its enduring significance stems from its role as the intellectual lingua franca of the ancient Mediterranean, fostering a unique cultural identity that transcended political boundaries.

During its classical flowering, Greek served as the medium for Homer's epic poems, the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, and the comedies of Aristophanes. It was the language in which Plato articulated his theory of Forms and Aristotle systematized logic, ethics, and natural science. Key advancements in mathematics by Euclid (c. 300 BCE) and physics by Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) were recorded in Greek, alongside the historical narratives of Herodotus and Thucydides. The Greek alphabet, adapted from Phoenician, introduced vowels, becoming the first truly phonetic writing system and facilitating widespread literacy and intellectual exchange throughout the Hellenistic world following Alexander the Great's conquests.
